246.title: The wedding date is written
246.hook: Sohila's first hymn speaks of death as a wedding day already fixed, asking friends for blessing (Gauri Deepaki, ang 12)
246.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite or sing Kirtan Sohila before sleep each night, and it is also recited when the Guru Granth Sahib is closed for the night and at the end of a Sikh funeral.

segments.voice: Yesterday, birha, the ache of separation; your line was longing is love too. Today, the bride again, and the day her waiting ends.

Before an old Punjabi wedding, the date is fixed and written down. Friends crowd around the bride with blessings, and in the custom the hymn draws on, a little oil is poured at the threshold. Everyone knows the day is coming. Sikhs sing a hymn at bedtime that uses exactly this picture. And the wedding it's talking about is not the one you'd expect.
screen: `THE DATE IS FIXED, WRITTEN.` → `FRIENDS BRING BLESSINGS.` → `OIL AT THE THRESHOLD.`

segments.voice: Kirtan Sohila is the Sikh night prayer, short hymns sung before sleep. It's also sung at the end of a Sikh funeral. Its first hymn is by Guru Nanak, in Rag Gauri Deepaki, on Ang 12, and its central line, in the original, is this: sanbat saahaa likhiaa mil kar paavahu tel. The year and the day are written; come together, friends, and pour the oil. Then: give me your blessings, so that I may meet my Lord. The bride is the soul. The groom is God. And the wedding day, fixed and written, is the day of death. It sounds heavy. It isn't meant to be. The hymn doesn't threaten, and it doesn't describe punishments. It turns death into a homecoming, the day the long-waiting bride from two days ago finally goes to her beloved. It adds that this summons comes to every house, every day, and so it asks us to remember the One who calls. Some readers hear why it belongs at night: sleep is a small rehearsal of letting go. You lie down not knowing, trusting the morning. At a funeral, the same words tell the family: this was not an ambush. It was a date, written, and a wedding. And the hymn is honest about its limit: it doesn't say when anyone's day is. Only that it's written, and that the wise way to live is to remember it gently, with friends and blessing.
screen: `KIRTAN SOHILA — THE NIGHT PRAYER.` · `SANBAT SAAHAA — THE DATE IS SET.` · `DEATH AS A WEDDING, NOT A THREAT.` · `EVERY NIGHT, A SMALL LETTING GO.` · then, large: `THE DATE IS WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: Let yourself remember, calmly, that your days are counted, as everyone's are; not to frighten yourself, just to see today clearly. Think of one thing you'd want to have done or said if you knew the date, a thank-you, an apology, a call, and hold it lightly. Let the breath be slow, the way it is before sleep.
Saahaa, the fixed wedding date. From Kirtan Sohila's first hymn: death pictured as the soul's wedding day, already fixed, met with friends and blessing rather than fear.
Your line: the date is written. Death as a homecoming, not a threat. Gently, until tomorrow.

247.title: From woman we are born
247.hook: Guru Nanak asks why she should be called lesser, from whom kings are born (Asa di Var, ang 473)
247.tomorrow: Ask about the light, not the caste
247.howItsDone: The Asa di Var is sung in many gurdwaras as part of the early-morning program; in Sikh congregations women and men sit together, eat together in the langar, and women may read from the Guru Granth Sahib and lead prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saahaa, the wedding date in Kirtan Sohila's first hymn; your line was the date is written. Today, a short verse with a very sharp question in it.

A baby is born, and in Guru Nanak's world, some said the birth had made the whole house unclean, the mother most of all. It was simply how things were said. Then a traveling teacher with a musician at his side sings a verse that asks one question, so plainly it's hard to argue with. It's in the Asa di Var, the morning ballad: from woman we are born.
screen: `A BABY IS BORN.` → `THE HOUSE CALLED UNCLEAN.` → `ONE PLAIN QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The Asa di Var is a long hymn sung in many gurdwaras in the early morning. On Ang 473 comes a salok by Guru Nanak. It begins with a drumbeat of one word, bhand, woman. In paraphrase: from woman we are born; in woman we are conceived; to woman we are engaged and married. Through woman comes friendship; through woman the way of the world goes on. When one woman dies, a man seeks another; through woman come our bonds with the world. Then the question, in the original: so kio mandaa aakheeai jit jameh raajaan. Why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? The salok goes on: from woman, woman is born; without woman there is no one at all. Only the One, the True Lord, Nanak says, is beyond woman. Notice where this sits. The verses just before it are about ritual impurity, sutak, the belief that birth made a house unclean. Guru Nanak answers that impurity lives in greed, lies and gossip, not in a newborn or a mother. So this isn't a greeting-card compliment. It's an argument, set in the middle of a debate about who is clean. Sikh practice reads the verse that way: in the sangat, women and men sit together and eat together in the langar, and women may read from the Guru Granth Sahib and lead prayers. Honesty belongs here too: life hasn't always matched the verse. But the verse is there, sung in the morning, still asking.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a woman in your life, a mother, a grandmother, a sister, a friend, a teacher, a colleague, and picture her face. Think of one thing she carried that nobody thanked her for, and hold that for a moment. Rest with the breath, and keep her in mind.
Bhand, woman. Guru Nanak's salok in the Asa di Var: everyone comes through woman, so why call her lesser, from whom kings are born?
Your line: why call her lesser. One plain question, hard to argue with. Day two hundred forty-seven, in the books.

248.title: Ask about the light, not the caste
248.hook: recognize the light in everyone and do not ask their caste (Asa, ang 349)
248.howItsDone: In the gurdwara langar, people of any background sit together in rows (pangat) on the floor and eat the same free meal; Sikh teaching rejects caste distinctions, though caste still shapes parts of community life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhand, woman, and Guru Nanak's question; your line was why call her lesser. Today, another label the Gurus refused to use.

Where are you from? What do you do? Where did you go to school? What's your last name? Those questions can be friendly. They can also be a way of sorting, placing someone on a ladder before you know them at all. In Guru Nanak's world, the big sorting question was caste, the group you were born into, which could decide whom you ate with and whom you married. Guru Nanak had a one-line answer: ask about the light.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOU FROM? WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `QUESTIONS THAT SORT.` → `THE BIG QUESTION THEN: CASTE.`

segments.voice: On Ang 349, in Rag Asa, Guru Nanak sings: jaanahu jot na poochhahu jaatee aagai jaat na he. Recognize the light, don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. Jot is light, the divine light Sikhs believe shines in every person. Jaat is caste, birth-group. And the verbs are the point: jaanahu, know, recognize; na poochhahu, don't even ask. Guru Nanak isn't only saying caste doesn't matter to God. He's saying don't make it the first question you put to a human being. The Gurus didn't leave this as a nice sentence. They built it into furniture and food. In the langar, the free kitchen, everyone sits on the floor in the same rows, the pangat, and eats the same meal, whoever they are. Tradition tells that Guru Amar Das asked visitors, even the Mughal emperor Akbar, to eat in the langar before meeting him. Later, tradition says, when Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa, the five who first stepped forward came from different castes and regions, and they drank amrit from one bowl. Caste didn't vanish from Punjabi life, Sikh life included, and the line still challenges the communities that sing it. But the rule on paper is clear, and it's short. Before you ask what someone's label is, see what's shining in them.

Look at them again in your mind: a face, a life, a light. Breathe in and silently say, see the light; breathe out, and stay here a while.
Jot, light, the divine light in every person. Guru Nanak's line in Asa: recognize it, and don't ask their caste.
Your line: see the light. One row, one meal, one bowl. See you next time.

249.title: Truth, and truthful living
249.hook: truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living (Sri Rag, ang 62)
249.tomorrow: Deeds as soil, the Word as seed
249.howItsDone: Sikhs quote Guru Nanak's line on truthful living (Ang 62) to describe the faith's emphasis on honest work, sharing and straight dealing in daily life, alongside remembering the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jot, the light in every person; your line was see the light. Today, a word the Granth uses for God, and a twist on it.

Two people. One can win any argument about honesty: quote the rules, spot every white lie, explain exactly what truth is. Then watch how that one treats the waiter. The other never talks about truth at all, but their word is solid, their yes means yes, and they return the extra change. Which of them has more truth in them? Guru Nanak answered in one line, on Ang 62. Today's word is sach.
screen: `WINS EVERY ARGUMENT.` → `THEN, THE WAITER.` → `WHICH ONE HAS TRUTH?`

segments.voice: Sach means truth, and in the Guru Granth Sahib it's bigger than facts. Sach, or sat, is one of the names of God. Satnam, the True Name, comes right at the start of the Granth. And Japji Sahib opens by saying, in paraphrase: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and, Nanak says, true forever. So truth isn't just something you tell. It's what's real, what lasts. Now the twist. On Ang 62, in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak sings: sachahu orai sabh ko upar sach aachaar. Everything is below truth; but higher still is truthful living. Aachaar means conduct, how you actually live. So there's something above even knowing the truth: living it. The Gurus didn't separate belief and behavior. A person who speaks beautifully about God and cheats at work hasn't reached the top of the line. A farmer who never read a book, and whose dealings are straight, might have. That's why the Sikh way leans so hard on the everyday: kirat karni, earning honestly; vand chhakna, sharing; the plain promise that your word is good. Truth, for the Gurus, is something you can see in a person's hands and hear in their bargains. It's also why this is hard. Knowing truth takes a clever mind. Living it takes every small moment of the day, including the ones nobody sees.

segments.voice: Think of one small truth you'd usually skip, not a big confession, just a little one, like I haven't read it yet, or that was my mistake, or I'm not fine, actually, or I can't make it. Picture saying it, simply and kindly, and notice what fear comes up, letting it be there. Then rest with the breath, steady and plain.
Sach. Truth, and in the Granth a name of God, what's real and lasts. And higher still than truth, Guru Nanak says, is truthful living.
Your line: truth, lived. Knowing it is good; living it is higher. That's day two hundred forty-nine.

250.title: Deeds as soil, the Word as seed
250.hook: make good deeds the soil and the Word the seed, and water it with truth (Sri Rag, ang 24)
250.howItsDone: Sikhs often cite Guru Nanak's years farming at Kartarpur as the model of a householder's life, joining honest work, remembering the Name and sharing, and his farming images are sung in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sach, truth; your line was truth, lived. Today, Guru Nanak takes that same idea out to a farm.

Ask any farmer in the Punjab, or anyone who's kept a tomato plant alive on a balcony: the seed is the easy part. A packet costs almost nothing. What decides the harvest is the ground you put it in, and whether you water it, day after day, when nothing seems to be happening. Tradition remembers Guru Nanak as a farmer in his last years, and his hymns are full of fields, plows and rain. On day 145 we heard one of them, the mind as plowman. Today, a different one: a whole spiritual life in a single line.
screen: `THE SEED IS THE EASY PART.` → `THE GROUND DECIDES.` → `NANAK THE FARMER.`

segments.voice: On Ang 24, in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak sings: amal kar dhartee beej sabdo kar sach kee aab nit dehi paanee. Make your deeds the earth, make the Word the seed, and water it every day with the water of truth. Then, in paraphrase: become that kind of farmer, and faith will sprout. Three parts. Amal, deeds, is the soil. Sabad, the Guru's Word, is the seed. Sach, yesterday's word, is the water, and nit means every day. Each needs the others. A beautiful seed in hard, stony ground won't grow: that's someone who hears wonderful hymns and changes nothing in how they act. Good soil with no seed is honest work with no remembering. And soil and seed with no water is a promising start that dries out by Thursday. The picture says something quiet about time, too. Farmers don't dig up a seed every morning to see if it's working. They water and wait. The next line says whoever farms this way comes to understand heaven and hell, and many readers hear in it that both grow from how you live. It fits the man who sang it. Tradition tells that after decades of travel, Guru Nanak settled at Kartarpur on the Ravi River and worked the land himself, with a community that farmed, sang and ate together. The teacher of the Word was also a man with dirt under his nails.
screen: `AMAL — DEEDS ARE THE SOIL.` · `SABAD — THE WORD IS THE SEED.` · `SACH — TRUTH IS THE WATER.` · `WATER AND WAIT.` · then, large: `DEEDS ARE THE SOIL.`

segments.voice: Imagine a small patch of ground: that's today. Choose one good deed to plant in it, a meal cooked for someone, a bill paid on time, an hour of help, a kind word to someone who won't expect it, and see yourself putting it in the ground. You don't need to watch it grow, only to water it; rest with the breath, patient as a farmer.
Amal, deeds, the soil of the spiritual life. Guru Nanak's farming picture in Sri Rag: good deeds are the ground, the Word is the seed, and truth, given every day, is the water.
Your line: deeds are the soil. No digging it up to check. Two hundred fifty days, and counting.

251.title: Rising spirits, good for all
251.hook: every Ardas ends asking chardi kala through the Name and the good of all
251.tomorrow: Why the Gurus kept others' hymns
251.howItsDone: Sikhs say the Ardas standing, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, at the end of services and at many moments of life, and it always ends by asking for chardi kala through the Name and sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amal: deeds are the soil. Today, the last of the Granth's great themes, and the last line of every Ardas.

The program at the gurdwara is ending. The whole congregation stands, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, hands folded. One person leads the Ardas, the standing prayer, remembering the Gurus, the martyrs, the sacrifices of centuries. It's long, and parts of it are heavy with history. Then it ends. Not with a request for our side to win, or for this group to prosper. It ends with a line that reaches past the door, past the city, to everyone alive. Today: sarbat da bhala.
screen: `THE CONGREGATION STANDS.` → `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS.` → `THEN, THE LAST LINE.`

segments.voice: The Ardas has grown over time. Its opening lines come from the Chandi di Var, which Sikh tradition attributes to Guru Gobind Singh, and later generations added the remembrance of the martyrs. It isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib, but Sikhs say it at gurdwaras, at home, before a journey, at weddings and funerals. It closes with these words: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Two phrases, each a whole teaching. Chardi kala means rising spirits: a spirit that keeps climbing, optimistic, unbroken, even in loss. And it's asked for through the Name, naam, not through luck or strength. Then: tere bhaane, by your will, sarbat da bhala. Sarbat means all, everyone, the whole. Bhala means good, well-being. The good of all. Not the good of Sikhs, or of the ones who agree. Everyone. Consider where this is said. The Ardas remembers people who were persecuted and killed. You might expect a prayer like that to end in anger. It ends in the good of all. It also closes this part of the path, the Granth's great themes: hukam and haumai, naam and nadar, the thieves and the virtues, maya, the gurmukh, sahaj, the bride and her longing, the written date, the light in everyone, truth lived, deeds as soil. And it all opens out here: a spirit that rises, and a wish that includes everyone.

segments.voice: Start close: picture someone you love and wish them well, then someone you barely know, the neighbor, the driver, then someone difficult, someone you'd rather not think about, if only a little. Then widen it: the street, the city, everyone. If you pray, you can say the Ardas's last words, sarbat da bhala; or simply, in your own words, good for everyone.
Chardi kala, rising spirits, asked through the Name in the closing wish of every Ardas, alongside sarbat da bhala, the good of all.
Your line: the good of all. It's a wish that leaves no one out. That's day two hundred fifty-one.

252.title: Why the Gurus kept others' hymns
252.hook: the Gurus placed the hymns of Hindu and Muslim saints of many castes inside the Guru's own book
252.howItsDone: Sikhs bow to the whole Guru Granth Sahib, including the Bhagats' hymns, as the Guru; the Bhagats' hymns are sung in kirtan in the same ragas as the Gurus' own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala, and the last words of the Ardas: the good of all. Today, a new stretch of the path, and the end of a week.

A holy book is being put together: the one its community will bow to, sing from, and one day call its living Guru. Into it go the poems of people from outside that community. A Muslim Sufi from the Punjab. A weaver from Benares. A leatherworker, from a caste others shunned. A barber. A farmer. Their words get the same place, the same music, the same honor as the Gurus' own hymns. That's what the Sikh Gurus did.
screen: `A HOLY BOOK IN THE MAKING.` → `POEMS FROM OUTSIDE IT.` → `THE SAME PLACE, THE SAME HONOR.`

segments.voice: Bhagat means devotee, a person of loving devotion to God; it comes from bhakti, devotion. In Sikh use, the Bhagats are the saints whose hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own. Tradition says Guru Nanak gathered some of their songs on his travels, and Guru Arjan compiled the first edition of the book, the Adi Granth, with their hymns inside it. Look who they were. Kabir, a weaver. Ravidas, a leatherworker. Sain, a barber. Dhanna, a farmer. Namdev, a calico printer. Sheikh Farid, a Sufi Muslim of the Punjab. Beside them, Brahmins like Ramanand and Jaidev. Hindus and Muslims, high castes and castes others shunned, from many parts of India. Why? The Gurus weren't collecting famous names. They kept hymns that sang what the Gurus sang: one God, the Name, love over ritual, and no respect at all for caste pride. Scholars add that the Gurus sometimes answered a Bhagat's verse with one of their own, which comes later in this stretch. So the book is also a conversation. That's this week's thread too: the written date, from woman we are born, ask about the light, truth lived, deeds as soil, the good of all, and now the Bhagats. Again and again, the Gurus opened the door wider than people expected. Truth, they seem to say, has many singers.
screen: `BHAGAT — ONE WHO LOVES GOD.` · `THE ADI GRANTH: THEIR HYMNS INSIDE.` · `WEAVER, BARBER, SUFI, BRAHMIN.` · `KEPT FOR WHAT THEY SANG.` · then, large: `TRUTH HAS MANY SINGERS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone very unlike you, another generation, another background, another faith or none, and recall one thing they said, wrote or sang that was simply true: a grandparent's proverb, a line from a song, something a coworker said once. Hold it a moment and let it be true, whoever said it, then rest with the breath.

Bhagat. A devotee; in Sikh use, the saints of many faiths and castes whose hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib. This week: the date is written, from woman we are born, the light, sach, deeds as soil, sarbat da bhala, bhagat.
Your line: truth has many singers. The Gurus listened for the song, not the singer's name. Week done; see you tomorrow.
